#### What type of PR is this?

/kind cleanup

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

UnprepareResources now uses claim info cache to get a list of claim names for the pod and falls back to the current approach - to get them from `pod.Status.ResourceClaimStatuses` using `resourceclaim.Name` API. This should help unpreparing resources even if pod.Status.ResourceClaimStatuses is empty.

The claim info cache is the authoritative record of what was actually prepared for a pod: `PrepareResources` stores a reference to every prepared claim keyed by claim name and pod UID and checkpoints it, so it survives `kubelet` restarts. 

Added a regression test covering a pod with an empty Status.ResourceClaimStatuses that references its claim via a template .

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/139772

This addresses the kubelet side of the issue (unprepare no longer depends on `pod.Status.ResourceClaimStatuses`). The broader problem - a client doing a full status PUT can drop status fields  (e.g. fields newer than its vendored `k8s.io/api`) - is wider than this fix, so the issue is intentionally left open to track that separately rather than auto-closed.

#### What type of PR is this?

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
`resourceclaim.IsForPod` can panic when `acceptPodGroupOwner=true` and the Pod has no scheduling group.

This is reachable in real code paths when `DRAWorkloadResourceClaims` is on. Callers pass the feature gate state straight through, but not every Pod is in a PodGroup. If ownership falls back to the PodGroup path, we hit a nil deref. Kinda nasty, easy to miss.

This patch adds the missing guard and returns a normal error instead.

Repro:
`cd staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation && GOWORK=off go test ./resourceclaim -run 'TestResourceClaimIsFor/Pod/accept-podgroup-without-podgroup' -count=1`

Before this change, that path panics.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR makes the etcd learner promotion path more resilient to transient client-side failures.

During investigation of intermittent etcd-join failures, I observed a scenario where MemberPromote() could return an error such as DeadlineExceeded, while the promotion may already have succeeded on the etcd side.

In that situation, kubeadm currently treats the promotion as failed and retries. However, if the learner has already been promoted to a voting member, subsequent calls can return below log:

```bash
etcdserver: can only promote a learner member
```

and kubeadm may continue retrying until the etcd-join phase fails.

This change re-checks the learner state after a failed MemberPromote() call. If the member is no longer a learner, kubeadm treats the promotion as successful and continues.

The fallback success path also re-lists members and adds the promoted member endpoint to preserve the existing endpoint update behavior that normally occurs when MemberPromote() succeeds and returns a response.

body:
I noticed that DRA `PrepareDynamicResources` / `NodePrepareResources` failures appear not to be propagated as pod sync errors in kubelet. As a result, the retry seems to happen on the regular pod resync interval instead of the pod sync error backoff path.

I would like to understand whether this is intentional, and if so, what the design rationale is.

**code path**

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05f19de8edd6557dbe35403f0501ac3e97f600b3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1585-L1597

When PrepareDynamicResources fails,the function returns early, but it does not appear to mark the PodSyncResult as failed, for example via either:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/05f19de8edd6557dbe35403f0501ac3e97f600b3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1498-L1522

This matters because if result.Error() == nil, the kubelet will re-process the pod after the default sync interval (60s–90s). Otherwise, the pod is placed into the backoff queue and will be retried sooner. In our experience, the first few PrepareDynamicResources calls sometimes fail, forcing us to wait through several default sync periods, which significantly increases pod startup latency.

body:
The first call to `UpdatePod` for a failed (rejected) pod sets `terminatingAt` but doesn't set `termitatedAt` because we need to run `SyncTerminatingPod` to clean up:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L803-L812

However, the first time we enter the pod worker loop, I'm pretty sure we end up saying the pod can never start, and exit the worker loop:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1234

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1180

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1047-L1049

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L1240-L1243

Unless I'm missing something, this looks like a bug with how we handle clean up in this case. But, if that cleanup isn't actually necessary, then maybe we can just set the `terminatedAt` timestamp immediately for the failed pod, which would cause it to be considered inactive.

Note: There is a test case that is suppose to cover this, but since the test uses a fake cache implementation that doesn't match the defaulting logic of the real cache, it skips over the code that generates the terminating sync status.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22e92c6a95c92329578154736a1e688f5ec35c87/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers_test.go#L750-L771

Copied from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136508#issuecomment-4411520959

body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR parallelizes per-pod reconciliation inside `GenericPLEG.Relist` in `pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go`. The previous implementation called `g.reconcilePodRecord` sequentially for every pod in `g.podRecords`; the new version first walks the pod records to compute the list of `PodLifecycleEvent`s and pending work, and then runs `g.updateCache` for each pod concurrently using `workqueue.ParallelizeUntil` with a constant cap of `plegMaxParallelism = 16` workers. Results are written to a pre-sized slice and applied serially afterwards, preserving the original event-aggregation, event-channel send, and `podsToReinspect` semantics.

The error-log path in `reconcilePodRecord` is also adjusted to handle a nil `pod` pointer (logging `podUID` instead of `klog.KRef(pod.Namespace, pod.Name)`), matching the corresponding log call in the new parallel path.

Resolves #139788

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Resolves #139788

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- The parallelism cap is defined as the unexported constant `plegMaxParallelism` in `pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go`.
- `updateCache` is the only call executed concurrently; event computation, `podsToReinspect.LoadAndDelete`, `podRecords.update`, and the `g.eventChannel` send remain serialized after the parallel section.
- The `results` slice is pre-populated with a placeholder error (`"context cancelled before processing"`) so a worker that never runs still produces a well-defined result that causes the pod to be re-inspected on the next relist, mirroring the existing `ctx` cancellation behavior in `reconcilePodRecord`.

## What this fixes

Two e2e tests have been flaking on any cluster that sets `--hostname-override` on kubelet (DigitalOcean/kops uses the droplet IP; some AWS+kops setups use the EC2 instance ID):

- `[sig-network] Networking Granular Checks: Services should function for service endpoints using hostNetwork`
- `[sig-network] Services should respect internalTrafficPolicy=Local Pod and Node, to Pod (hostNetwork: true)`

Both tests compare a response from a hostNetwork pod against the Kubernetes node name. The response comes from agnhost's `/hostname` endpoint, which calls `os.Hostname()`. On distros where `--hostname-override` diverges from the system hostname, `os.Hostname()` returns neither the k8s node name nor any predictable truncation of it.

## Fix

Use `spec.nodeName` via the Downward API — the only unambiguous source of the k8s node name:

- Inject `NODE_NAME=spec.nodeName` into hostNetwork endpoint pods via Downward API (both in `createNetShellPodSpec` and the service.go test pod).
- Add `echoNodename = "envvar?var=NODE_NAME"` and switch hostNetwork dial paths to use it via `endpointDialCommand()`.
- `EndpointHostnames()` now inserts `p.Spec.NodeName` for hostNetwork pods.
- For UDP/SCTP, the dial relay sends the request as raw bytes — HTTP query-string syntax can't be reused. `echoNodenameUDP = "envvar%20NODE_NAME"` percent-encodes the space so `url.ParseQuery` at the relay decodes it to `"envvar NODE_NAME"` as the agnhost UDP handler expects.
- `DialFromNode` updated symmetrically for both HTTP and UDP.
- Add `execNodenameTest()` in `util.go` — no FQDN truncation since node names are always unqualified.

Non-hostNetwork code paths are entirely unchanged.

## Prerequisites (all merged)

| PR | Description |
|----|-------------|
| #138737 | Add `/envvar` endpoint to agnhost, bump to 2.65.0 |
| kubernetes/k8s.io#9608 | Promote agnhost:2.65.0 staging → prod |
| #139756 | Bump agnhost image references to 2.65.0 |

## Local smoke test

```
/envvar?var=NODE_NAME  → kind-control-plane   (matches spec.nodeName ✓)
/hostname              → agnhost-downward      (diverges — proves the bug ✓)
echoNodenameUDP decode → "envvar NODE_NAME"    (url.ParseQuery %20 → space ✓)
```

I encounter unexpectedly high CPU utilisation (sitting around 10-15% as reported by `top`) in a Kubernetes cluster using CRI-O as the container runtime.

Although the desired outcome is for the cluster to manage multiple deployments using a network fabric (CNI), the high-CPU condition is replicable before the network fabric and (non-system) containers/pods are created.

Based on sampling on the node, approximately 600 syscalls per second to `epoll_pwait` occur from the `kubelet` process, and I feel that that is an unexpectedly large rate.

I had a guess/theory that polling-based PLEG might account for this.

However: enabling `EventedPLEG` for the Kubelet in combination with enabling runtime container events in `cri-o` (both following guidance from the [Kubernetes EventedPLEG switching guide](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/switch-to-evented-pleg/)) does **not** seem to reduce either the CPU utilisation or the number of `epoll_pwait` syscalls.

For an effectively empty, inactive cluster, I would anticipate lower CPU usage - five percent or lower.

I do not know whether to expect a reduced number of `epoll_pwait` syscalls -- they seem exessive to me, but perhaps they fulfil an important role.

I am able to replicate this after using `kubeadm init` to initialise a basic single-node Kubernetes cluster with a fairly minimal Kubelet configuration, using `cri-o` as the (autodiscovered; no explicit configuration) container runtime on the node host.

body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

The structured DRA allocator post-processes each claim's resolved configs and
clears `DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests` to `nil` when a config applies
to every request, taking advantage of the "empty Requests means all requests"
semantic.

The condition it used was a length comparison:

    len(config.Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests)

This is not equivalent to "this config covers every request in the claim". A
`Requests` entry can be a subrequest reference of the form
`"<request>/<subRequest>"`. A config scoped to N subrequests of a *single*
request has N entries, so when the claim happens to have N top-level requests
the lengths match and the config's `Requests` was cleared — silently widening a
narrowly-scoped config to the entire claim.

This PR clears `Requests` only when the config covers every top-level request,
either by the request's name or by the request's selected subrequest. The check
reuses the same matching rules already used when the configs are built, so the
existing behavior for a single request with subrequests (where clearing is
still correct) is unchanged.

The fix is applied to all three allocator variants (`stable`, `incubating`,
`experimental`), which are kept in sync.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:

Fixes #139803

**Special notes for your reviewer**:

A regression test (`claim-config-scoped-to-subrequests-of-one-request`) is added
to the shared allocator test suite. It uses a claim with two top-level requests
where one config is scoped to two subrequests of the first request; the config
must remain scoped instead of being widened to the whole claim. The test fails
against the previous length-based check and passes with this change, and runs
against all three allocator implementations.

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**

```release-note
NONE
```

body:
## What this PR does / why we need it

On cgroupv2 systems, `kubepods.slice` cpu.weight is derived from
absolute nodeAllocatable milliCPU, which scales linearly with core
count. This causes `kubepods.slice` to grossly outcompete `system.slice`
and other top-level slices for CPU on high-core machines.

**Root cause:** In `getCgroupConfigInternal()`, CPUShares is set via
`MilliCPUToShares(allocatableMilliCPU)` an absolute value that grows
with core count. When converted to `cpu.weight` via `getCPUWeight()`,
this produces a weight far above the system default of 100.

**Fix:** In `getCgroupConfig()`, when running on cgroupv2, CPUShares is
scaled proportionally to `(allocatable / totalCapacity)` so that
`kubepods.slice` gets a cpu.weight reflecting its actual CPU fraction.

## Reproduction

16-core node, `system-reserved=cpu=8` (50/50 split):

Before fix
kubepods.slice  cpu.weight = 313   # pods get 3x more CPU than kernel threads

system.slice    cpu.weight = 100   # baseline
After fix
kubepods.slice  cpu.weight = 20    # proportional to 50% CPU allocation

system.slice    cpu.weight = 100   # baseline unchanged


On a 64-core node with system-reserved=cpu=32, the imbalance is 25x
(cpu.weight=2500 vs 100), causing kworker starvation, I/O degradation,
and potential livelock.

## Impact

- **cgroupv2 only** — fix is gated behind `IsCgroup2UnifiedMode()`
- **cgroupv1 unaffected** — no change in behavior
- **Per-pod weights unaffected** — only top-level kubepods cgroup is changed
- **Behavior change** — pods get less CPU weight vs system processes
  compared to before, but this is the correct proportional behavior

## Testing

- Added unit test `TestGetCgroupConfigProportionalCPUWeight` covering:
  - 16-core node, 50% reserved
  - 64-core node, 50% reserved  
  - 16-core node, small reservation
- All existing `pkg/kubelet/cm` tests pass
- Race detector clean (`go test -race`)
- Manual verification on 16-core cgroupv2 kubeadm cluster confirmed
  cpu.weight drops from 313 → 20 after fix

## Related issues

Fixes #139790
Related to #125409

body:
### What happened?

The DRA structured allocator post-processes allocated configs to drop a `DeviceAllocationConfiguration.Requests` list to `nil` when the config "applies to all requests" (the *empty means all* semantic). It decides this with a length comparison:

```go

for i := range allocationResult.Devices.Config {
    if len(allocationResult.Devices.Config[i].Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests) {
        allocationResult.Devices.Config[i].Requests = nil
    }
}
```

`len(config.Requests) == len(claim.Spec.Devices.Requests)` is **not** equivalent to "this config covers every request in the claim", because `config.Requests` entries may be sub-request references of the form `"<request>/<subRequest>"`  the allocator matches them that way a few lines earlier:

```go
subRequestName := fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s", request.Name, subRequest.Name)
if slices.Contains(config.Requests, subRequestName) { ... }
```

A config that references **N sub-requests of a single parent request** has `len(config.Requests) == N`. If the claim has **N top-level requests**, the lengths match even though the config covers only one of them  so its `Requests` is cleared and the config is silently re-scoped to **every** request in the claim.

The same defect is present in all three production implementations:
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/experimental/allocator_experimental.go` (the cleanup loop)
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/incubating/allocator_incubating.go`
- `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/stable/allocator_stable.go`

### What did you expect to happen?

A config that references only sub-requests of one request should remain scoped to that request. `Requests` should be cleared to `nil` (the "applies to all" form) only when the config actually covers **all** top-level requests in the claim.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add this case to the shared table in `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/internal/allocatortesting/allocator_testing.go` (`TestAllocator`) and run `go test ./structured/internal/experimental/ -run 'TestAllocator/repro-config-subrequests-not-all'` (fails identically for `incubating` and `stable`):

```go
"repro-config-subrequests-not-all": {
    features: Features{PrioritizedList: true},
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claim(claim0).withRequests(
            requestWithPrioritizedList(req0,
                subRequest(subReq0, classA, 1),
                subRequest(subReq1, classB, 1),
            ),
            deviceRequest(req1, classA, 1), // second top-level request, unrelated to the config
        ).withConfigs(objects(
            // references BOTH sub-requests of req0 only; must NOT apply to req1
            deviceClaimConfig([]string{req0SubReq0, req0SubReq1}, deviceConfiguration(driverA, "foo")),
        )),
    ),
    classes: objects(class(classA, driverA), class(classB, driverB)),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, pool1, driverA,
        device(device1, nil, nil), device(device2, nil, nil),
    )),
    node: node(node1, region1),
    expectResults: []any{allocationResultWithConfigs(
        localNodeSelector(node1),
        objects(
            deviceAllocationResult(req0SubReq0, driverA, pool1, device1, false),
            deviceAllocationResult(req1, driverA, pool1, device2, false),
        ),
        []resourceapi.DeviceAllocationConfiguration{{
            Source:              resourceapi.AllocationConfigSourceClaim,
            Requests:            []string{req0SubReq0, req0SubReq1}, // expected: stays scoped to req0
            DeviceConfiguration: deviceConfiguration(driverA, "foo"),
        }},
    )},
},
```

Device allocation comes out exactly as expected (`req-0/subReq-0` → `device-1`, `req-1` → `device-2`); the **only** difference is the config scope:

```text
expected: Requests: ["req-0/subReq-0", "req-0/subReq-1"]
actual:   Requests: nil      # == applies to ALL requests, including the unrelated req-1
```

body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature
/kind api-change
/sig scheduling
/sig node

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Alpha implementation of [KEP-5963: DRA Device Compatibility Groups](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5963).

This PR adds a driver-authored `compatibilityGroups` field to each `device.consumesCounters[]` entry of a `ResourceSlice`. Two devices drawing from the same counter set may be co-allocated only if their groups intersect (share at least one name); a device with no groups is only co-allocatable with other no-group devices. The scheduler enforces this during allocation — as an additional predicate inside the DRA structured allocator's existing backtracking search — and records a per-counter-set snapshot of the allocated device's groups on `ResourceClaim.status`, so subsequent allocations evaluate against the value captured at allocation time rather than a possibly-mutated `ResourceSlice`.

The whole feature is guarded by a new alpha feature gate `DRADeviceCompatibilityGroups` (off by default; kube-apiserver and kube-scheduler) and builds on `DRAPartitionableDevices`. With the gate disabled there is no behavior change.

The change is organized into reviewable commits:
- the `DRADeviceCompatibilityGroups` feature gate;
- the API fields + generated code (internal and `v1`/`v1beta1`/`v1beta2`, applyconfigurations, protobuf, openapi, swagger);
- apiserver validation + feature-gated field stripping (with ratcheting on update);
- structured-allocator enforcement (rolling per-counter-set group intersection, status snapshot, backtracking rollback, and version-skew skipping);
- scheduler-plugin plumbing (gate → allocator features, and snapshot read-back through `AllocatedState`).

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5963

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

- **API shape vs. the KEP:** the KEP specifies the status snapshot as `map[string][]string`, but Kubernetes protobuf cannot represent a repeated map value (`go-to-protobuf` silently drops the `repeated` flag on a map value), so it is implemented as `map[string]CompatibilityGroupList`, where `CompatibilityGroupList` wraps a `Groups []string`. The semantics are identical; only the wire/JSON shape of the status field differs. The KEP README will be updated to match.
- Allocator enforcement is implemented in the `incubating` and `experimental` allocator variants; the `stable` variant skips devices that declare groups it cannot evaluate (version-skew safety).
- Nil-matching is strict: an unset field, an explicit nil, and `[]` are equivalent and mean "no groups"; a no-group device is only co-allocatable with sibling no-group devices.
- Test coverage in this PR: unit tests for the group-intersection predicate; end-to-end allocator scenarios across all three variants (compatible / incompatible / cross-claim snapshot read-back / feature-disabled skip); field validation; and apiserver field-stripping for both the slice field and the claim-status snapshot, including ratcheting. Integration tests (gate enable/disable round-trip, snapshot-authoritative-over-mutated-slice), an e2e test (fake driver advertising mutually exclusive MIG/vGPU groups), and a scheduler_perf workload are planned as follow-ups per the KEP test plan.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Added alpha support for DRA device compatibility groups, guarded by the new 
`DRADeviceCompatibilityGroups` feature gate (off by default). 
DRA drivers can declare opaque `compatibilityGroups` on each `device.consumesCounters[]` 
entry of a ResourceSlice, and the scheduler only co-allocates devices drawing from the same 
counter set when their declared groups intersect, moving detection of incompatible co-allocation 
from preparation-time failure to scheduling-time rejection.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

- KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/5963-device-compatibility-groups

body:
### What happened?

On a 64-CPU box, with cgroups v2, I set up kubernetes 1.35 with system-reserved=cpu=32, so reserve "half the CPU for non-kubernetes stuff".

This results in a kubepods.slice structure like:

```
 CGROUP                                      cpu.max       cpu.weight
 kubepods.slice                              max 100000     2500
    kubepods-burstable.slice                  max 100000      ???
 ...
```

The value for `kubepods-burstable.slice` will vary depending on your pod configuration (it was 633 for me) but it doesn't really matter here.

`kubepods.slice` is a top level cgroup, which means it competes with weight 2,500 against other top level groups will generally all have weight 100. This means that when a bustable pod demanding "all" the CPU are competing against a kernel threads (for example), they get _25x_ the CPU that kernel thread does.

This has real impacts when the pod load itself requires kworkers to do work: e.g., to process disk completions: the pods themselves starve their own kworkers, leading to very performance or even livelock when the kernel wq exhausts all its slots.

What is the basis for setting the top-level kubepods.slice weight so high? This only gets worse with increasing core counts.

It does not make sense to me that the weight scales up with more cores: as in the above example we ask for a 50/50 split pod and system CPU, let the weight of the top-level kubepods cgroup keeps going up with more cores.

`--enforce-node-allocatable=pods` can paper this over in some cases, by preventing the pods from bursting across all CPUs, but this breaks as soon as the pods are using CPU affinity or under static CPU allocation.

pods should compete fairly with a appropriate `cpu.weight`

### What happened?

`StreamWatcher.Stop()` can send a spurious `watch.Error` event to the result channel instead of closing it cleanly.

`Stop()` closes the HTTP response body via `source.Close()`, causing the blocked `Decode()` in `receive()` to fail with `"http2: read on closed response body"`. Since `IsProbableEOF` does not recognize this error string, `receive()` attempts to send the error as a `watch.Error` event.


### What did you expect to happen?

The `"http2: read on closed response body"` error should be treated as EOF.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start a watch against the API server
2. Read from `ResultChan()` in a consumer goroutine
3. Call `Stop()` from a separate goroutine while the consumer is still reading
4. Observe that ~50% of the time, the consumer receives a `watch.Error` event with message `"unable to decode an event from the watch stream: http2: response body closed\") has prevented the request from succeeding"` before the channel closes.

At this point, both `<-sw.done` and `sw.result <- Event{Error}` are ready in a `select`, and per the Go spec one is chosen at random — so roughly 50% of the time, a spurious error event is delivered to the consumer.

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR adds integration and performance benchmarks for gang preemption ( WorkloadAwarePreemption ).
It introduces new performance tests in `test/integration/scheduler_perf/workload_preemption/` that benchmark the scheduler's behavior under different gang preemption workloads:

1. `preemption-performance-basic.yaml` : Tests basic gang preemption.
2. `preemption-performance-affinity.yaml` : Tests gang preemption with node affinity constraints.
3. `preemption-performance-podgroups.yaml` : Tests preemption when multiple podgroups are involved.

The benchmarks simulate low-priority pods distributed across nodes and then schedule high-priority gangs that require preempting some of the low-priority pods. This helps measure the throughput and latency of the preemption code path.

*Update:* Parameterized the high priority groups count in `preemption-performance-podgroups.yaml` and replaced the massive `1000Nodes_5LowPriorityGangs_1PreemptorGang_EvictAllGangs` scenario with `100Nodes_50LowPriorityGangs_10PreemptorGangs_10Pods` to scale down the workload size and prevent test execution timeouts.

title: api-server does not always refetch JWKS on unknown key ID

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

body:
### What happened?

We're performing regular key rotation of our signing keys used to sign tokens issued by our OIDC provider. Unfortunately the api-server does not properly refetch new signing keys.

The openid specification states that:
> The signer can begin using a new key at its discretion and signals the change to the verifier using the kid value. The verifier knows to go back to the jwks_uri location to re-retrieve the keys when it sees an unfamiliar kid value.

Source: https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#RotateSigKeys

However, as written above the api-server does not comply with that. Currently the api-server is using the coreos/go-oidc v2 library which only reloads keys when the cache-control max-age is reached. 

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected api-server to comply with the openid spec and immediately refetch keys if an unknown kid is seen.

This behaviour has already been changed in v3 of coreos/go-oidc library with https://github.com/coreos/go-oidc/pull/259. Keys are immediately refreshed if an unknown key id is seen.

However, this change has the potential to DDOS the issuer when someone brings an invalid token or a token meant to be for another cluster if the api-server (or the coreos/go-oidc library) does not rate limit such requests (as far as I can tell go-oidc does not rate limit). So some additional work might be needed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I can try to put together a reproducer later but I don't think it is needed at this point.

### Anything else we need to know?

On #sig-auth slack channel I found [this](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0EN96KUY/p1667778735333849) old thread from 2022 describes a similar/related problem. I believe all recent Kubernetes versions are affected by this bug. This would be fixed by #134454

### Context
In the recent SIG-Node CI subgroup meetings (6/10/2026), we discussed the need to better track our CI stability and test degradation over time. 

Currently, we are manually tracking the status of our Testgrid dashboards in a [Spreadsheet Tracker](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IwONkeXSc2SG_EQMYGRSkfiSWNk8yWLpVhPm-LOTbGM) before every meeting. We document the current status (Passing/Flaky/Failing) of the jobs and link them to tracking GitHub issues, but doing this manually makes it hard to see historic data and trends.

### Goals
We would like to gather community input on what metrics, tooling, and dashboards we should use to automate this monitoring. For starters, we can try to answer questions like:
* How long has a specific test or job been failing?
* Is a recurring failure caused by the same error or a new regression?
* How long do SIG-Node CI bugs remain open?
* How many `important-soon` bugs do we currently have, and what is their average resolution time?
Please recommend any more you think of, open to all suggestions!!

### Existing Efforts & Ideas
* We dug up an [existing dashboard started by dims](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-metrics/failures-latest.html?include=node&sort=days&asc=0), but we need to determine how persistent this data is, how it's generated, and how we can best utilize or adapt it.
* Could we leverage existing Kubernetes `test-infra` tooling (like BigQuery metrics/[Kettle](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/kettle/README.md), `k8s-triage` in the [aggregated failures dashboard](https://storage.googleapis.com/k8s-triage/index.html?sig=node)) to automate the data we currently put in our manual spreadsheet?

### Call to Action
We are opening this issue to invite ideas from the CI/CD community. 
1. What metrics do you think are most important for us to track?
2. Are there existing dashboards or tools in the Kubernetes ecosystem we should be leveraging?
3. Any volunteers interested in helping build out or maintain this reporting?

Please drop your thoughts and suggestions below!

title: WatchList initEvents uses a different semantic comparing to the old List+Watch approach

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

body:
### What happened?

When reflector uses List+Watch, it request ANY version by setting RV=0. [Code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0cd4e13c69be9ec44267efeaf9acfd90ef4af5f5/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L1126-L1130)
When reflector uses WatchList, it always requests MostRecent version. [Code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0cd4e13c69be9ec44267efeaf9acfd90ef4af5f5/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L1135-L1144)

When the apiserver watch cache is temporarily falling behind (due to high load):
1. A controller with old ListWatch approach is more resilient to temporary staleness given it uses RV=0 .
2. A controller with WatchList with MostRecent semantic approach can suffer longer bootstrap time due to multiple attempts and timeouts. 

More details about the 2nd scenario:
1. Controller (e.g. KCM) initialize a WatchList request with MostRecent
2. APIServer queries etcd to get the latest RV=X
3. APIServer times out after waiting 3s and return 429 to client.
4. Controller retries another WatchList request with MostRecent
5. APIServer queries etcd to get the latest RV=Y (Y>X)
6. APIServer may already have X, but can't catch up with Y in 3s, it returns 429 to client
7. This repeats multiple rounds until the watch cache catches up. During this time, the controller can still hold the leadership because the lease update is cheap and always succeeds even when other resource watch cache is falling behind, but makes no progress for a couple minutes.


### What did you expect to happen?

From resilient to temporary staleness perspective, controller initialization using WatchList should not be worse than the old List+Watch behavior.

A few options to consider:
1. WatchList in Reflector use RV=0 instead of RV="". (easiest and matching old behavior)
2. WatchList can wait longer than 3s before giving up
3. Even when watch cache is not up to date, WatchList starts to serve synthetic events immediately from watch cache and dispatch new etcd events that apiserver receives until it catches up with RV=X. Then it sends the bookmark event. The initEvents no longer contain pure synthetic ADD events.
4. Everything is same as option 3 above except that WatchList starts to serve synthetic events from watch cache after waiting for up to 3s.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138728#issuecomment-4445545871 should be able to reproduce

body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Two distinct gRPC connection leak paths cause kubelet memory to grow monotonically until restart:

1. **handler.go**: `connectClient` unconditionally created a new client without checking if one was already registered for the same resource name and socket path. On every subsequent registration, a new client and ListAndWatch goroutine were created while the previous one was orphaned because it could no longer be looked up in the clients map. **Fix**: deduplicate by looking up an existing client before creating a new one in `connectClient`.

2. **client.go**: `Connect` establishes a gRPC connection via `dial()`, but if the subsequent `handler.PluginConnected()` call fails, the connection is never closed. The leaked file descriptors accumulate over time, particularly when plugins restart frequently or fail during registration. **Fix**: use a named-return defer to close the connection and reset `c.grpc` and `c.client` on any error after `dial` succeeds.

This can be observed in production when a device plugin repeatedly registers against its own socket (e.g. during rapid re-registration), causing goroutines and file descriptors to grow until kubelet is restarted.

Added two unit tests in `handler_test.go` to cover each leak path:
- `TestDuplicateRegistration`: verifies repeated `connectClient` calls with the same name and socket create exactly one client.
- `TestConnectFailureCleanup`: verifies no client is registered and the gRPC connection is closed when `PluginConnected` fails.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fix: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/124716

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fix kubelet memory leak caused by orphaned gRPC connections when a device plugin registers against an existing socket, and close the connection if the handler rejects the plugin during Connect.
```

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Adds a new declarative-validation tag, `+k8s:dependentForbidden`, the inverse of the existing `+k8s:dependentRequired`: when the tagged (trigger) field is set, the named sibling field must **not** be set. The error is reported at the sibling field with a `Forbidden` type and `dependentForbidden` origin. Like `dependentRequired`, dependencies are one-directional, the tag may be repeated to forbid multiple siblings, and updates are ratcheted (the check is skipped when neither side's set-ness changed).

This expresses common mutual-exclusion rules between sibling fields declaratively. For example, a Linux-only field that may not be combined with `windowsOptions`:

```go
// +k8s:dependentForbidden("cgroupOptions")
WindowsOptions *WindowsSecurityContextOptions `json:"windowsOptions,omitempty"`
```

Since `dependentRequired` and `dependentForbidden` share all parsing and codegen logic, the generator is consolidated into a single mode-based `dependencyTagValidator`, mirroring how `requirednessTagValidator` covers `required`/`optional`/`forbidden`. Only the validator name, error type, origin, and docs vary by mode.
